arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Horwich argued that the statutory structure treats firearm types as distinct elements.
Mr. Fisher argued that no defendant received more than ten years without a machinegun finding.
Justice Scalia questioned whether the statutory language supports treating weapon type as an element.
Justice Breyer asked why the Court should depart from its prior interpretation of similar statutes.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case tests how courts interpret federal firearm statutes. It asks if specific weapon types define separate crimes or act as sentencing factors.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the Court to treat the machinegun provision as a separate crime requiring a new jury verdict.
The government wants the Court to treat the machinegun provision as a sentencing factor that judges may consider.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case argues that moving firearm type provisions signals they are distinct elements, not sentencing factors.
The government argues that recidivism and weapon type traditionally function as sentencing factors, not elements.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case determines whether defendants face mandatory minimum sentences based on weapon type without a separate jury finding. It clarifies the boundary between criminal elements and sentencing enhancements in federal law.
